이건:남:Igor.text: 이건 (利建, Igeon) joins 利, meaning beneficial, with 建, to establish, painting the hope that someone will build things of lasting value and bring good wherever their efforts take root — a life spent constructing benefit for others, not just for oneself. Spoken aloud, the name is brisk and clean: a short "i" opening into the firm, grounded "geon," crisp yet warm, easy for English speakers to say. Abroad, it settles comfortably near "Igor," giving someone a familiar echo while keeping its own true, hopeful shape.
이건:남:Igor.short: One who builds lasting benefit for others

우빈:남:Otavio.text: 우빈 (佑彬, Ubin) joins 佑, meaning to help, with 彬, meaning shining, painting the image of someone whose brightness becomes a support to others — a light that steadies rather than dazzles. Parents choosing it often dream of a boy who lifts people up simply by being near them. Spoken aloud, the name flows gently: the rounded "oo" opens into the crisp, clean "bin," soft yet confident. Abroad, it sits comfortably alongside Otavio, both carrying an easy, open rhythm that rolls naturally off the tongue.
우빈:남:Otavio.short: A shining light that helps others

한울:남:Paulo.text: 한울 (漢蔚, Hanul) joins the wide, steady flow of the Han River with the lushness of things flourishing along its banks, holding a hope that this person's life will spread out broad and abundant, never running dry. Alongside cousins like 한결, 지한, 하울, and 시울, it shares that same river-warmth. Spoken aloud, Hanul is soft and open, its vowels rolling easily, faintly echoing the familiar shape of Paulo to English-speaking ears, gentle and easy to carry anywhere.
한울:남:Paulo.short: A life flourishing wide like a river

아윤:여:Ayu.text: 아윤 (雅潤, Ayun) joins 雅, refined and elegant, with 潤, lustrous, painting someone whose grace carries a natural shine — a hope that she moves through the world with quiet polish, elegant not by effort but by inner glow. Spoken aloud, the name feels light and open, its vowels rounding softly from "ah" to "yoon," easy on the tongue, gentle in the ear. It shares its warm rhythm with names like 수아 and 서윤, and abroad, as Ayu, it keeps that same soft familiarity, easy for others to say and remember.
아윤:여:Ayu.short: Refined elegance with a lustrous glow

이담:여:Intan: Idam carries a quiet kind of beauty: 利 for benefit and blessing, 潭 for a deep, still pond. Together they suggest a life that nourishes those around it, calm on the surface but full underneath. Spoken aloud, Idam is soft and open, the vowels rounding gently like water settling after a ripple. That same stillness echoes in Intan, their English name — both carry the sense of something precious quietly gathered and held.

이담:여:Indah.text: 이담 (利潭, Idam) joins beneficial (利) with a deep, still pond (潭), picturing a person as a quiet gathering place where good things settle and calm runs deep. The hope woven in is of someone whose presence steadies others, a source that others can draw benefit from without ever running shallow. Spoken aloud, Idam is soft and clean, its open vowels unfolding easily, the crisp *d* giving it a gentle, confident lift. Abroad, it echoes comfortably alongside Indah, familiar on the tongue.
이담:여:Indah.short: A calm, deep source of goodness

우나:여:Wulan: Una carries a gentle wish: 佑 (u) meaning "to help," and 娜 (na) meaning "beautiful," together forming someone made to bring graceful support into the world. Spoken aloud, Una flows in two open, unguarded syllables—soft as a breath, with nothing sharp to catch on, much like the ease found in Jiu, Seou, Yuna, or Yena. Fittingly, it echoes gently into Wulan, her English name, both carrying that same light, open warmth.
채하:여:Cahaya: Chaeha carries color into a river—彩 for brightness, 河 for flowing water—so the name suggests light caught in a current, always moving, never dull. Spoken aloud, it opens softly: "chae" crisp and bright, "ha" wide and easy, like a breath let out. That same brightness echoes in Cahaya, which means light—so someone named Chaeha carries radiance in two languages, one flowing like a river, the other shining like a lamp.

기쁨:여:Gita.text: 기쁨 (Gippeum) — above all, this is the native Korean word for joy itself, carried whole and unbroken as a name, so that someone given it holds happiness not as a wish added on but as their very name. The hope folded inside is simple and full: that light-heartedness, delight, and gladness might follow them through their days, and that their presence might stir the same in others. Spoken aloud, it feels soft yet crisp, opening gently on breathy consonants before settling into a round, warm close — much like how "Gita" lands easily on English-speaking ears.
기쁨:여:Gita.short: Joy carried as a given name

기쁨:여:Kirana.text: 기쁨 (Gippeum) — above all, this is the native Korean word for joy, for the light, bubbling happiness that rises without effort. Given to a girl, it carries the hope that she will be a source of gladness in every room she enters, and that her own heart will stay light even through hardship. Spoken aloud, it feels soft yet crisp, opening on a gentle "gi" and closing on a warm, rounded "ppeum." Abroad, its rhythm echoes pleasantly alongside Kirana, familiar and easy on the tongue.

라윤:여:Rahayu.text: 라윤 (羅潤, Rayun) unfolds like silk catching light — 라 carrying the sense of fine fabric spreading open, 윤 giving it a lustrous sheen, so together the name holds the hope of someone whose presence unfurls

세은:여:Sekar: Se-eun carries a quiet grandeur: se (世), the whole wide world, joined to eun (恩), grace and kindness — a wish that someone might meet that vast world gently, and be met by it in kind. Spoken aloud, it flows softly, the open "se" easing into the tender hum of "eun," like a breath settling. That same warmth echoes into their English name, Sekar, its bright, rounded sound carrying forward the same gentle, open-hearted spirit.

빛나:여:Vina.text: 빛나 (Bitna) — above all, this is the native Korean word for "to shine," carrying the hope that someone will glow with their own light, radiant and unmistakably present in any room they enter. It's a name parents choose wishing brightness not just of appearance but of spirit, someone whose presence lifts others. Spoken aloud, it feels light and lively, the crisp "bit" giving way to the open, gentle "na," soft on the tongue. Abroad, it echoes comfortably into "Vina," familiar and easy to carry.

이담:여:Widya: Idam carries a quiet, glimmering image: benefit and blessing (利) settling like clear water into a still pond (潭), a place where good things gather and deepen rather than rush away. Spoken aloud, it's soft and open — the bright "ee," the gentle "dam" — like a breath held calmly. Much like Widya, the name Idam suggests depth beneath simplicity, someone whose presence feels steady, generous, and quietly luminous.

지은:여:Citra.text: 지은 (智恩, Jieun) joins wisdom and kindness into a single quiet wish: that someone would carry a clear, thoughtful mind alongside a gentle, giving heart, never one without the other. Spoken aloud, the name feels soft and close, its syllables tapping lightly with open vowels and a smooth, unhurried rhythm that seems to settle rather than rush past. Abroad, its rounded ending echoes gently in "Citra," making it easy for new ears to catch and remember.
지은:여:Citra.short: Wisdom paired with a kind heart

이은:여:Irma.text: 이은 (利恩, Ieun) joins two quiet strengths: 이, meaning beneficial, and 은, meaning kindness or grace, together shaping a hope that someone will move through life bringing good to others, a presence whose very nearness leaves things better than before. Spoken aloud, the name is gentle and clear, its two open vowels rolling softly without hard edges, easy on the tongue and warm in the ear. Abroad, it settles comfortably beside Irma, close enough in sound to feel instantly familiar.
이은:여:Irma.short: A person whose kindness brings benefit to others

예강:여:Eka.text: 예강 (睿康, Yegang) joins wisdom with peace, painting the hope of someone whose mind stays clear and thoughtful while their spirit remains calm and untroubled — a person who might meet life's noise with quiet steadiness rather than worry. Spoken aloud, the name flows gently: the soft "ye" opens bright and clean, sliding into "gang," which lands crisp but rounded, never harsh. Abroad, it echoes comfortably alongside Eka, its sound easy for new ears to hold, familiar yet distinctly its own.
예강:여:Eka.short: Wise mind held in lasting peace

빛나:여:Vira: Bitna, written purely in native Korean sound, means "shining" — a name that carries the simple, radiant hope that someone will glow with their own light, brightly and without needing translation. Spoken aloud, it opens softly on the lips, then brightens with a crisp, clean edge, much like a spark catching. That same gleam carries into Vira, echoing light and life, so the shine follows someone across languages, unbroken.
이담:여:Winda: I-Dam carries a quiet richness: 利 for benefit and grace, 潭 for a deep, still pond—together suggesting a calm depth from which good things naturally flow. Spoken aloud, it opens softly and closes clear, the vowels wide and unhurried, like water settling after a ripple. It sits gently alongside names like Jaei and Sodam, sharing that same clean, breath-like ease. In Winda, that same sense lingers—a name that moves quietly, yet carries far.
청아:여:Cempaka: Cheonga carries a name built from doubled clarity—cheong's clear brightness and a's refined grace—as if someone wished for a person untouched by murkiness, elegant in the plainest sense of the word. Spoken aloud, it opens softly and closes clean, each syllable rinsed and unhurried, like water over smooth stone. That same clear-eyed brightness echoes in Cempaka, a flower prized for its pure, carrying fragrance—fitting, since Cheonga was always meant to feel effortlessly transparent and lovely.

바다:남:Bambang.text: 바다 (Bada) — above all, this is the native Korean word for the sea, carrying the hope that someone might grow with a heart as vast, deep, and unshaken as the ocean itself, holding room for every tide of joy and hardship life brings. Spoken aloud, it flows smoothly, its open "ah" vowels rolling like gentle waves, soft yet clear. Abroad, its easy rhythm sits comfortably beside the name Bambang, both warm and welcoming to the ear, familiar from the very first hello.
바다:남:Bambang.short: A heart as vast and deep as the sea

재진:남:Dedi.text: 재진 (才眞, Jaejin) joins talent (才) with truth (眞), naming someone whose gifts are genuine rather than borrowed or performed — a hope that whatever ability they carry will be real, honest, and wholly their own. Spoken aloud, it moves lightly: the open "ae" softens into a crisp, clean "jin," giving the name a bright, tidy sound, quick on the tongue yet grounded. Abroad, its rhythm sits comfortably beside "Dedi," making it easy for new ears to catch and remember.
재진:남:Dedi.short: Genuine, true talent that is authentically one's own

하람:남:Fajar.text: 하람 (河藍, Haram) joins the river's steady flow with indigo's deep, quiet blue, carrying a hope for someone whose spirit runs wide and constant, holding a color that only deepens with time rather than fading. Like 하준, 하

종건:남:Joko.text: 종건 (宗建, Jonggeon) joins the root of origin, 宗, with the act of establishing, 建, carrying the quiet hope that someone will become a founding pillar—one who honors where they come from while building something lasting and true for those who follow. Spoken aloud, the name feels grounded yet open: the crisp "jong" gives way to the soft, breathy "geon," a rhythm of firmness and ease. Abroad, it settles comfortably alongside Joko, sharing that same easy, open-voweled warmth.
종건:남:Joko.short: One who founds a lasting legacy

무영:남:Mulyono: Muyoung carries a quiet strength: 무, meaning robust, grounds someone in sturdy resolve, while 영, meaning glory, lifts that strength toward shining achievement. Together they express the hope that a person will meet life with steady, unshakable power that naturally earns honor and light. Spoken aloud, Muyoung flows smoothly—an open, breathy "moo" easing into the crisp, bright "young," soft yet confident. Fittingly, it echoes the rising, hopeful sound of their English name, Mulyono.

부건:남:Purnama.text: 부건 (副建, Bugeon) joins 부 (副), meaning to assist, with 건 (建), meaning to establish, painting the hope of someone who helps raise up what is lasting — a steady hand behind every foundation, content to build rather than boast. Spoken aloud, the name is quick and clean, its consonants crisp against open, rounded vowels, giving it a grounded, confident rhythm. Abroad, it settles comfortably beside Purnama, close enough in sound to feel like an easy echo, familiar from the very first hearing.
부건:남:Purnama.short: A steady helper who builds lasting foundations

세환:남:Setiawan.text: 세환 (世煥, Sehwan) joins 世 "the world" with 煥 "bright," carrying the hope that someone will shine brilliantly enough to light up the whole world around them, bringing warmth and radiance wherever they go. Spoken aloud, the name flows smoothly—soft consonants easing into open vowels, ending on a gentle nasal hum that lingers pleasantly. It shares a bright, clean rhythm with names like 세현 and 지환, and abroad it

우찬:남:Umar.text: 우찬 (佑燦, Uchan) joins help and shine into a single wish: that someone would move through life as a source of light for others, aiding those around them while radiating warmth of their own. It carries the same gentle spirit found in names like 시우 and 유찬. Spoken aloud, it feels crisp yet soft, opening on a rounded "oo" and settling into a bright, clean "chan" — a sound not far from the familiar Umar, which may ease its way into new tongues abroad.
우찬:남:Umar.short: One who helps others while shining bright

윤수:남:Yusuf.text: 윤수 (潤秀, Yunsu) joins 潤, lustrous, with 秀, outstanding — a name that wishes for someone whose brilliance never dulls, whose gifts shine with a natural, unforced polish rather than a hard glare. It sits alongside names like 도윤, 시윤, 수현, and 수호, sharing that gentle luster. To say it is easy: two clean syllables, "yoon" soft and rounded, "soo" crisp and open, flowing together smoothly. Abroad, it echoes comfortably near the familiar name Yusuf, an easy bridge between worlds.
윤수:남:Yusuf.short: Outstanding brilliance with a lasting shine

이든:남:Indra: Ideun carries no hanja—just pure native Korean sound, chosen for how it feels rather than what it encodes character by character. Said aloud, it opens softly and closes clean: the bright "ee," the gentle "deun," nothing sharp or heavy. It sits comfortably beside names like Ian and Ijun, sharing that same warmth. Paired with the English name Indra, there's a quiet echo too—both carry a breath of quiet strength, something steady beneath the softness, wished for whoever wears it.

수한:남:Surya.text: 수한 (秀漢, Suhan) joins outstanding excellence with the grandeur of the Han River, holding the hope that someone would grow both remarkable and expansive — a person whose gifts run as deep and steady as a great river carving through a city, quietly shaping everything it touches. Spoken aloud, the name feels smooth and open, its soft "s" easing into wide, breathing vowels, landing gently like water finding its course. Abroad, it settles comfortably alongside Surya, familiar on the tongue yet wholly its own.
수한:남:Surya.short: Outstanding spirit as vast as a river

이담:여:Imelda: 이담 (利潭, Idam) joins 利, beneficial, with 潭, a deep still pond, painting the quiet hope that someone's presence will bring lasting good to those around them, like calm water that nourishes without demanding notice. It carries a settled, generous spirit rather than loud fortune. Spoken aloud, Idam is soft and open, the vowels rounding gently while the ending stays crisp and clean. It shares gentle rhythm with 소담 and 예담, and abroad it echoes comfortably alongside Imelda, familiar yet quietly its own.
소담:여:Soledad: 소담 (昭潭, Sodam) joins bright with pond, picturing calm water lit from above—a hope that someone might hold both light and stillness together, a clarity that doesn't ripple away under pressure. It suggests a person steady enough to reflect what shines near them without losing their own quiet depth. Spoken aloud, Sodam is soft and rounded, its open vowels settling gently, much like 소율 or 예담. Abroad, it echoes comfortably alongside Soledad, familiar on the tongue.
바다:여:Bernadette: 바다 (Bada) — above all, this is the native Korean word for the sea itself, given in the hope that someone might carry within them something as vast, deep, and endlessly renewing as the ocean. It's a name of open horizons and quiet strength. To say it aloud is to feel two soft, open vowels roll forward like gentle waves — nothing sharp, nothing hidden, just clarity and breadth. Abroad, it settles comfortably near "Bernadette," easy for new ears to catch and hold.
도혜:여:Dolores: 도혜 (道惠, Dohye) joins 도, meaning path, with 혜, meaning kindness, holding the hope that someone will walk through life guided by a compassionate heart, choosing gentleness as their true direction. Spoken aloud, it carries a soft, rounded warmth, opening on that clear "do" and settling into the tender hush of "hye," easy and graceful on the tongue. Abroad, it sits comfortably alongside Dolores, its sound familiar to English speakers, even as its own meaning remains rooted in path and kindness.
빛나:여:Beverly: 빛나 (Bitna) — above all, this is a native Korean word built from "bit," meaning light or radiance, joined to "na," carrying the sense of emerging or coming forth. Together they hold the hope of someone who shines, whose brightness naturally rises and becomes visible to others — light not just possessed, but actively unfolding. The sound matches that meaning: crisp at the start, then softening into open, easy vowels that glow rather than snap. Abroad, it settles comfortably beside Beverly, close enough in rhythm to feel instantly familiar.
상은:여:Charmaine: 상은 (祥恩, Sangeun) joins 祥, auspicious fortune, with 恩, kindness, painting a life graced by good omens and a gentle, generous heart—someone meant to carry blessing outward through warmth toward others. Spoken aloud, it flows softly: the rounded "sang" settles into the open, breathy "eun," crisp yet unhurried, like a quiet exhale. It shares its rhythm with names such as 상희, 상아, 하은, and 은서. Abroad, its sound echoes gently in "Charmaine," offering a familiar handle without borrowing its meaning.
기쁨:여:Queenie: 기쁨 (Gippeum) — above all, this is the native Korean word for joy itself, carried whole into a name, as if someone's very presence were meant to be a source of delight and gladness for those around them. It kin to 슬기, 기은, 예쁨, 미쁨, sharing that soft, rounded "-eum" ending common in native Korean names. Spoken aloud, it opens brightly, then closes gently — crisp yet warm. Abroad, as Queenie, its sound settles just as easily on the tongue, familiar and welcoming.
빛나:여:Vilma: 빛나 (Bitna) — above all, this is the native Korean word meaning "to shine," carrying the quiet hope that a person will glow with their own light, radiant and unmistakably themselves, needing no one else's flame to be bright. It shares its shine with names like 은빛나 and 예빛, all catching light in different ways. Spoken aloud, it is soft yet crisp, opening on a bright vowel before closing gently — light and clear, like the name Vilma feels abroad, familiar and easy to carry.
인호:남:Ignacio: 인호 (仁浩, Inho) joins benevolence with broadness, painting the hope of a heart generous enough to hold others gently while reaching wide into the world—kindness that never narrows, spirit that never shrinks. Spoken aloud, it flows easily: a soft "in" settling into an open, breathy "ho," the whole name light on the tongue yet warm in tone. Abroad, it sits comfortably beside Ignacio, familiar enough to greet new ears without losing the gentle broadness carried within.
호림:남:Policarpio: 호림 (浩琳, Horim) brings together broad, expansive vastness with the quiet luster of fine jade, painting a hope for someone whose spirit stretches wide yet carries a polished, precious core beneath it. Spoken aloud, the name moves smoothly — a soft opening breath into a crisp, clean close, its vowels open and easy on the tongue. Abroad, it settles comfortably alongside Policarpio, the two names sharing a similar warm, rolling rhythm that makes introductions feel natural in either language.
성빈:남:Servillano: 성빈 (成彬, Seongbin) joins 成, to achieve, with 彬, shining, painting the hope of someone who grows into accomplishments that give off their own quiet radiance — success not just earned but luminous, refined rather than loud. Spoken aloud, Seongbin flows smoothly, its soft consonants and open vowels giving it a gentle, polished rhythm, much like cousins 민성 and 은성. For English speakers, it echoes pleasantly close to Servillano, an easy bridge between two worlds.
태오:남:Teodoro: 태오 (泰旿, Taeo) joins 태 for greatness with 오 for brightness, painting the wish for someone who carries themselves with a broad, generous grandeur while shining steadily on those nearby — a light that doesn't flicker, but glows wide and warm. Spoken aloud, 태오 feels open and clean, its two syllables landing softly like a breath let out, with nothing sharp or hidden in it. Abroad, it settles easily into the familiar shape of Teodoro, making it simple to say and quick to feel like home.
우찬:남:Ubaldo: 우찬 (佑燦, Uchan) joins 우, to help, with 찬, shining, painting the quiet image of someone destined to support others while radiating their own bright light — a helper whose presence itself illuminates a room. Spoken aloud, the name moves smoothly from a rounded, breathy "oo" into a crisp, open "chan," giving it a bright, confident rhythm that feels both gentle and strong. Abroad, it settles comfortably alongside the name Ubaldo, sharing that same warm opening sound.
보근:남:Virgilio: 보근 (寶根, Bogeun) joins 보, treasure, with 근, root, picturing something precious anchored deep in the ground where it can never be lost or washed away — the hope that a person's worth grows steady and lasting, not fleeting. Spoken aloud, it feels soft yet grounded, the open "bo" easing into the crisp, quiet close of "geun," like a breath settling. Abroad, it sits comfortably near Virgilio, familiar enough to greet easily, while carrying its own rooted, treasured meaning.
이도:남:Wilfredo: 이도 (利道, Ido) joins 利, meaning beneficial or advantageous, with 道, meaning path or way, together shaping the hope that someone will walk a road that brings good to others, a life whose direction itself becomes a gift to those around them. Spoken aloud, Ido flows softly and quickly, its open vowels leaving the mouth easy and unguarded, gentle as a breath. Abroad, its clean shape sits comfortably alongside Wilfredo, sharing that same friendly, easy-to-say brightness.
바다:여:Valeria: 바다 (Bada) — above all, this is the native Korean word for the sea itself, and the hope folded into it is spacious: a life as wide, deep, and unstoppable as the ocean, someone who can hold many currents within her and still remain whole. Spoken aloud, it opens easily on the tongue, both syllables bright and unclipped, the vowels wide open like a horizon. For someone abroad, it happens to echo faintly the shape of Valeria, a small bridge between two worlds, though its true depth remains the sea alone.
빛나:여:Berenice: 빛나 (Bitna) — above all, this is the native Korean word meaning "to shine," carrying the hope that someone will glow with their own inner light, radiant and unmistakably present wherever they go. It shares its warmth with names like 은빛나 and 예빛, all glowing with that same light, and echoes softly with 유나 and 예나 in rhythm. Spoken aloud, it is bright and clean — a crisp consonant opening into wide, easy vowels, quick and luminous like a spark. Abroad, it settles comfortably near Berenice, familiar on the tongue.
이담:여:Hilda: 이담 (利潭, Idam) joins the character for benefit or advantage with the character for a deep, still pond, painting a picture of quiet water that gives generously to all around it — a wish for someone whose calm depth brings good fortune to others rather than draining away. Spoken aloud, Idam is gentle and grounded, its open vowels settling like ripples coming to rest. It shares a gentle kinship in sound with the name Hilda, making it easy to carry comfortably abroad.
이봄:여:Ivonne: 이봄 (Ibom) — above all, this is native Korean for "this spring," a name that carries the hope of new beginnings, fresh light, and gentle renewal, as if someone arrived exactly when the world was softening into bloom. The sound matches that warmth: two light, open syllables, "i" bright and quick, "bom" rounded and calm, easy to say in a single breath. Abroad, it settles comfortably near Ivonne, familiar on the tongue while still holding its own quiet, springlike meaning.
관우:남:Cuauhtemoc: 관우 (寬佑, Gwanu) joins generosity with helpfulness, painting the picture of someone whose wide, open heart naturally extends aid to others — a name carrying quiet hope that a person will grow into a steady, giving presence, the kind others lean on. Spoken aloud, it flows softly, the "gwan" rounding warmly before settling into the bright, open "u" — gentle, unhurried, easy to say. Abroad, it echoes pleasantly alongside Cuauhtemoc, sharing a similar rhythm that makes it feel instantly familiar on foreign tongues.
우빈:남:Octavio: 우빈 (佑彬, Ubin) joins the quiet strength of helping with the elegant glow of shining, painting the picture of someone meant to assist others while carrying their own gentle radiance — a helper whose presence naturally brightens a room. Spoken aloud, the name flows smoothly, its soft consonants and open vowels giving it a warm, easygoing lilt, gentle yet clear. For anyone abroad, it settles comfortably alongside Octavio, sharing a similar rhythm that makes it easy on the ear in either language.
하늘:남:Pablo: 하늘 (Haneul) — above all, this is the native Korean word for "sky," carrying a wish for someone whose spirit stays wide, boundless, and unclouded, reaching as far as the eye can see. It shares its open, breathing sound with names like 하준 and 하람, all beginning with that same soft "ha." Spoken aloud, Haneul flows gently — light consonants, wide vowels, nothing sharp or heavy. Abroad, it settles comfortably beside "Pablo," easy for new tongues, yet always echoing that vast, quiet sky.
우승:남:Ulises: 우승 (佑承, Useung) joins 佑, to help, with 承, to carry on, holding the hope that someone will lift others up while faithfully continuing what came before—a steady bridge between generations. The sound flows warm and easy: the rounded "oo" opens gently into the crisp "sung," soft yet firm on the tongue, much like siblings 시우, 연우, 승현, and 승우. Abroad, it settles comfortably beside Ulises, its rhythm familiar enough to feel like home in either language.
원희:여:Ruoxi: 원희 (元喜, Wonhui) joins the character for foremost with the character for glad, so the name carries a quiet wish: that this person stand first in joy, or that gladness itself come first in her life, above all else that follows. Spoken aloud, Wonhui flows softly, opening wide on "won" and closing gently on the bright "hui," a warm, easy sound. Abroad, this pairs comfortably with Ruoxi, sharing that same light, welcoming ring.
마야:여:Mengyao: 마야 (馬野, Maya) unites 마, carrying the sense of words, with 야, an open field, painting the image of a wide meadow where language runs free—a hope that someone will speak with ease, gather thoughts like grass under open sky, and always find room to express what stirs inside them. Spoken aloud, the name feels soft and unhurried, its vowels open and warm, ending on a gentle exhale. Abroad, it settles comfortably beside Mengyao, familiar on the tongue, easy to carry across languages.
윤하:여:Yuhan: 윤하 (潤河, Yunha) joins 潤, lustrous, with 河, river, painting the image of a river catching light—glimmering, generous, ever-flowing. The hope folded into it is of a life carried forward with quiet brilliance, someone whose presence nourishes others the way a river sustains everything along its banks. Spoken aloud, Yunha is soft and clear, its open vowels sliding gently like water over stone.
